abstract.p: Living materials, which are either made of and by living cells or synthetic with programmable elements catered to cells within, are environmentally responsive and can self-repair, allowing for controlled and predictable interactions with biological systems. Such features can also be achieved in purely synthetic materials by using chemical approaches to create dynamic and responsive materials that can undergo programmed changes, that can be remodelled by cells in a predictive way, sense their microenvironment and report back, or respond to remote triggers to rearrange in physical or chemical ways. In this Review, we discuss synthetic approaches to design such cell- and environment-responsive living materials, with a particular focus on their application in cancer. We highlight how synthetic and systems biology approaches can be implemented in the design of synthetic living materials and outline key cancer-related applications, including modelling of tumour heterogeneity, the tumour microenvironment and tumour evolution in response to therapy. Finally, we emphasize the importance of inclusive designs that should be based on an understanding of how health and disease manifest and impact humans from all racial and ethnic backgrounds, skin colors, sex, and genders.

abstract.title: Short summary
abstract.p: Synthetic living materials are dynamic and responsive, actively interact with and integrate into biological systems, and predictably evolve. This Review discusses the engineering of synthetic living materials and their applications in cancer biology.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The term living materials, which was first mentioned in 19691, refers to biomaterials that can mimic or interact with dynamic biological systems. Living materials have thus far been defined as materials made from living cells, primarily microbes, engineered to produce biomolecules with specific properties2–8. Living materials can also refer to composites of cells and materials, wherein the materials can be synthetic or produced by mammalian cells, microbes9–15 or plant cells16. Living materials, however, may also include materials made from synthetic precursors that are simultaneously dynamic and responsive, actively interact with and integrate into biological systems, and, unlike biological living materials, can evolve over time in a predictable or programmable manner. Such synthetic living materials can respond to external triggers, report on cellular activity, or self-replicate in response to a stimulus or a biological system.

Extracellular matrix (ECM)-derived materials have provided inspiration to create living materials that interact with cellular systems in predictable, dynamic and evolving ways. Re-purposing individual or combinations of ECM components, such as collagen or Matrigel, has allowed the culture of living cells in environments that can be re-modelled by cells; however, the native ECM, or materials made from reconstructed ECM proteins, may not provide the predictable and evolvable features possible with synthetic counterparts. Alternatively, materials can be engineered with more sophisticated properties to allow active integration of the material with cells, alongside predictable evolution of the cellular-material system; for example, photo-degradable materials can direct organoid growth, mimicking natural development and regeneration processes 17, materials with specific enzyme sensitivities allow for single cell analysis with spatiotemporal control 18, and magnetically responsive materials can control the stiffness of gels and thereby cancer cell transformation 19. Such dynamic, responsive and evolvable materials may be applied as engineered tissue replacements, to provide interactive tissue-like functions (for example, in soft robotics), as responsive therapies, and as model systems to study human physiology and diseases, such as fibrosis, wound healing and cancer.

Synthetic living materials may also be applied to understand, diagnose, and treat cancers. The tumour microenvironment (TME) is spatially complex and evolves over time in response to treatment and disease progression. A materials system with dynamic and evolvable properties may thus enable the classification and identification of TME-related processes that drive the disease to signal and commence intervention and/or interrupt disease progression. The scale, components, and dynamics of such a system are complex, and many of the underlying control rules are not yet understood. Therefore, its design and control will require concerted efforts of materials scientists, engineers, systems biologists and synthetic biologists (FIG. 1) to define and create synthetic living materials that can sense, report on and respond to a dynamic and heterogeneous tumour milieu to improve our understanding of the processes that drive tumour cell properties and disease progression, provide feedback and inform cells or controllers, and drive innovative solutions to the most complex problems in cancer.

In this forward-looking Review, we discuss the design of synthetic materials that can change in ways that mimic cancer progression (Figure 2a) and that contain therapeutics to respond positively to those changes. We highlight the convergence of materials design, synthetic biology, engineering, and systems biology to create material-cell systems that recapitulate relevant tumour biology, outlining the current state of living materials in the context of cancer, and we call out future milestones to address grand challenges in cancer biology with next-generation living materials.

sec.title: Living materials synthesis strategies
sec.p: When engineering cell-biomaterial interactions, a biomaterial can be designed to actively elicit a specific cellular response and/or play a passive role, in which it is predictably altered by embedded cells (Figure 2b). In addition, external physical or chemical stimuli, such as light, an electromagnetic field, mechanical force, or a change in pH or temperature, can trigger programmable, predictable and dose-dependent changes in biomaterials to direct specific material and cell responses on demand (FIG. 2b–h , Table 1).

sec.title: Photo-reactive chemistries
sec.p: Light-catalyzed chemical reactions can be exploited to enable user-defined material modifications, such as a change in stiffness, with high spatial and temporal resolution20 (FIG. 2). In particular, photo-reactive chemistries can be applied to create such dynamic biomaterials21. For example, bioactive molecules, tethered to polyethylene glycol (PEG) hydrogels, can be released on-demand using photolabile protecting groups, such as ortho-nitrobenzyl22. Similarly, two-photon activation of photocaged thiols, immobilized within a hydrogel matrix, can be used to create 3D spatial gradients of epidermal growth factor (EGF), enabling a model of breast cancer cell chemotaxis23.

Photo-reactive chemistries can also be used to modify the physical properties of a material, such as crosslink density or stiffness, which affect cell behavior independently of biochemical cues24,25. For example, biomaterials with photosensitive groups undergo light-triggered crosslinking or degradation to induce stiffening or softening, respectively, in user-defined regions26–28. Using distinct wavelengths of light, hydrogel stiffness and ligand density can then be independently altered, on demand, in the presence of cells. Single-photon excitation of photoactivable compounds restricts spatial control to a 2D plane; however, multi-photon excitation using fast-pulsed red or far-red lasers achieves 3D spatial resolution at scales close to 1 μm 29,30,52. For example, light can be applied to sequentially stiffen and soften a PEG hydrogel to model tumour progression in the presence of 3D-cultured breast cancer cells31.

Moreover, optogenetic techniques can be used to activate mechano-sensitive ion channels in cells32. Combining such intrinsic (optogenetic) and extrinsic (via the living material) tools allows control over the local mechanical interactions between cells and their microenvironment. This can be achieved by applying synthetic biology tools, for example, by engineering synNotch receptors to interact with specific ligands presented by a biomaterial to trigger an encoded biological response 33.

sec.title: Cell-responsive materials
sec.p: Cells engage in dynamic reciprocity with the TME, where cells produce and modify ECM, which in turn presents signals back to the cells 34. During homeostasis, the ECM is subjected to continuous and tightly controlled remodelling, mediated by cell-secreted enzymes and their inhibitors. Matrix degradation affects how the ECM presents ligands to cell receptors and sequesters and releases growth factors 35. These changes to ECM composition also affect local mechanics, which can directly impact cell function through mechanotransduction and lead to further changes in ECM deposition and remodelling 36. Disruption of this dynamic balance is a hallmark of cancer.

In tumours, cancerous and resident stromal cells also alter the ECM, which can be recapitulated in protein-based materials in vitro; for example, cell tension causes alignment and stiffening of fibers in collagen gels37–39. Similarly, synthetic biomaterials can be designed that allow cells to stiffen their surroundings; for example, both cell-produced enzymes35,40 and cell-induced strain41, can trigger the formation of new crosslinks, causing an increase in biomaterial stiffness. However, synthetic biomaterials do typically not interact with cell-released proteins that crosslink the ECM42. Alternatively, peptide-based or protein-derived materials, contain specific peptide sequences that bind cells or that are degradable43–45, can be integrated in a biomaterial that is not cell- or ECM protein-adhesive. Such ECM-protein binding sites could also serve as nucleation points for crosslinking.

Cells typically apply forces to their surroundings as they move and divide, which can be accounted for by using force- or strain-sensitive materials that crosslink under deformation (shear, compression, and ultrasound) 41,46. Such force-catalyzed crosslinking materials are inspired by mechanophores, which are typically tension-sensitive confined rings (isomerization) or weak covalent bonds (scission)47. Force-sensitive materials have been demonstrated using externally applied force; however, this concept could be extended to cell-applied tensions if the crosslinks were sufficiently sensitive.

Biomaterials can also be designed to passively degrade over time; for example, cell-mediated biomaterial degradation can be achieved by including crosslinks susceptible to enzymes (for example, matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), cathepsins or disintegrin and metalloproteinases (ADAMs)) naturally secreted by cells to remodel their ECM. Degradability may be essential for the intended function of specific biomaterials; for example, neural stem cells cultured in 3D PEG-based hydrogels can only maintain their stem-like properties if MMP-degradable sites are included48. Cell-degradable crosslinks can also be used to control the degree of cell migration within a biomaterial49 and to release bioactive factors or therapeutic drugs50 by altering biomaterial porosity. Porosity can spatially confine cell morphology and tune cell function or allow cell movement through a 3D scaffold. Thus, the porosity of synthetic matrices can be exploited to approximate cell confinement during migration through the native matrix, a defining event in cancer metastasis51.

Similarly, pH-triggered changes can be used to create cell-responsive biomaterials, which may be particularly useful for applications in cancer, as the TME is generally acidic owing to hypoxia and a reliance on glycolytic metabolic pathways. In contrast to enzymatic changes of a biomaterial, which are often permanent, pH-induced changes may be reversible under specific oxidation-reduction conditions.

Living materials can be designed to directly affect cell behavior, as well as evolve as a function of cell deposition of new ECM. For example, ECM secreted by cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) drives stiffening of the TME during cancer progression (FIG. 2). Accordingly, co-cultures of CAFs and tumour cells or organoids within a hydrogel matrix can model progressive tumour stiffening through CAF deposition of new ECM into the hydrogel matrix52. Whether through the use of light (extrinsically controlled) or mechanophores (cell-initiated), such living materials can serve as in vitro models to investigate tumour response to the stiffening and softening ECM during disease progression.

sec.title: Dynamic crosslinks and viscoelastic materials
sec.p: To mimic the physical properties of the highly viscous and dynamic ECM, hydrogel biomaterials can be engineered with dynamic crosslinks, also called adaptable or reversible crosslinks. Such crosslinked biomaterials have viscoelastic properties, where stress-relaxation occurs in seconds to hours, reflecting the time scales in native tissues 53. The viscoelastic properties of materials have substantial effects on the phenotype and behavior of cells. In addition, dynamic crosslinks, formed by reversible covalent bonds or physical interactions, facilitate cell spreading, migration and cell-cell interactions 54,55.

Cells displaying amoeboid-type behavior, such as when their cytoskeletal machinery is altered 56 or through loosely crosslinked collagen gels 57, migrate independently of matrix degradation and must push through pores in the ECM. Many cell types, including cancer cells, likely use a combination of amoeboid- and mesenchymal-type (adhesion- and contractility dependent) mechanisms for migration and matrix remodelling58,59. In cancers originating in epithelial tissues, the onset of metastasis is thought to depend on a phenotypic epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) 60. Transitions between mesenchymal and amoeboid migration modes may allow cancer cells to adopt to changing tissue microenvironments encountered during metastasis. For example, confinement (for example, in a biomaterial or ECM pores) may trigger a transition to an amoeboid state, which increases cortical actin contractility, enabling a cancer cell to move forward 61. By contrast, transition to a mesenchymal phenotype with lower actin contractility may be advantageous for unconfined migration62,63. Dynamic crosslinks can be designed to be broken by interacting cancer cells or CAFs and then reform or ‘self-heal’ afterwards on a minutes to hours timescale53,64.

Dynamic crosslinks can be formed using covalent or physical chemistries that determine the kinetics of breaking and reformation and, thus, viscous relaxation times65,66. Boronates 67–69, hydrazones 70–73 and thioesters 74,75 can be implemented as covalent, reversible crosslinks, which typically involves reversible addition or exchange reactions. The chemical components can be selected to control relaxation rates, determined by on/off and equilibrium kinetics on the covalent crosslink. For example, aliphatic aldehydes or benzaldehydes can be used to create fast- (τ1/2 ~ 10 s) or slow- (τ1/2 ~ 2400 s) relaxing biomaterials; here, fast-relaxing scaffolds enable increased cell spreading 76.

Viscoelastic materials based on reversible physical crosslinks typically rely on supramolecular interactions, including hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interactions, electrostatic interactions, metal-ligand interactions and guest-host interactions 77. Cyclodextrin guest-host interactions with adamantane or azobenzene can be implied to create nanoporous hydrogels for cell culture with tunable viscoelasticity 78,79. Peptide fibers, mimicking the fibrous structure of the ECM, can be engineered to self-assemble through physical crosslinks into tunable viscoelastic biomaterials; here, by varying the numbers of ureido-pyrimidinone (UPy) groups that are available for crosslinking individual peptide fibers and that dimerize through hydrogen bonding in physiological conditions, stress-relaxation times can be precisely controlled 80.

Double or interpenetrating networks created from interlocking two independently crosslinked polymer networks allow semi-independent control over viscous and elastic properties 78,81,82. Specifically, one network is formed through covalent crosslinks and the second network through physical crosslinks; here, the covalently crosslinked network has a higher influence on the elasticity, and the physically crosslinked network on the viscosity of the final biomaterial. As with elasticity, light can be used for spatiotemporal control of viscoelasticity using strategies based on diothiolane or cyclodextrin-azobenzene crosslinks 79,81.

sec.title: Future designs
sec.p: Living materials could also be designed with more complex, multifunctional building blocks, with both passive and active modalities that respond to physical and chemical signals and dynamically mediate reciprocal interactions with cells (FIG. 2). For example, an external trigger could be used to stiffen a hydrogel co-culture of CAFs and tumour cells, resulting in mesenchymal-like CAF migration (Figure 2b). Migrating CAFs would then break MMP-sensitive crosslinks, resulting in the release of a hydrogel-embedded, bioactive factor that induces a phenotypic transition of CAFs and/or tumour cells. Alternatively, biomaterials could be modified with magnetic nanoparticles; the application of an external electromagnetic field could then trigger the formation of additional nucleation sites to reversibly enhance material stiffness and, subsequently, alter the phenotypes of 3D-cultured cancer cells 19.

Tumours are acidic relative to the homeostatic body pH, which can be exploited in drug delivery; for example, dynamic polymersomes can be designed to become unstable and release cargo in acidic environments 83. Similarly, dynamic biomaterials can be engineered that can swell and contract, or alter their crosslinking density in different pH environments (Figure 2c). For example, temperature can regulate the swelling behavior of polymer gels, which can be exploited in Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) to trigger a liquid-solid transition 84. Temperature-sensitive particles can also be triggered to swell and release cargo upon near-infrared (NIR) (external) heating to treat tumours 85. pH- and temperature-sensitive hydrogels have been limited to therapeutic delivery applications thus far; however, pH- and temperature-sensitive biomaterials could also be valuable in creating shape-changing materials, stiffening materials or to mimic the dynamic and pH-variable TME.

Both the magnitude and kinetics of changes to a biomaterial microenvironment can be influenced by the simultaneous application of external and chemical stimuli, integrated with additional functional responses. For example, reciprocal interactions can be programmed into living materials that have been bioprinted into complex geometries, which evolve in coordination with the differentiation of adipose-derived stem cells (ASCs) towards bone or cartilage tissue86. This concept could be extended to cancer, as ASCs can function like CAFs in the TME87. Furthermore, biomaterials or interacting cells can be engineered to report on and respond to specific biological events to generate dynamic, closed loop systems. For example, a biomaterial could be engineered to respond to features of tumour-supportive immune cells by transitioning to an immune-cell activating microenvironment. In addition, biomaterials with electromagnetic properties may act as sensors or reporters of cell behavior, while dynamically responding to and co-evolving with cells during cancer progression.

sec.title: Systems biology to study and design living materials
sec.p: A pervasive challenge in the design and analysis of living materials is the breadth and complexity of environmental signals that influence cell behavior and, in turn, the many mechanisms by which cells influence their environment. Regardless of whether there is a mechanistic understanding of these regulatory processes, visualizing or exploring how a single change to a living material affects the individual components of a tissue and its integrated overall properties remains difficult. Understanding systems-level properties of living materials is critical, but remains a multi-factorial challenge . For example, the mechanical properties of the tissue, the composition of the ECM, the composition, localization and concentration of soluble factors, and the dimensionality of a living material may shape the responses of cells embedded within it, and each of these can, in turn, affect the response to one another88–90. Together, this makes the space of possible effects immensely large. Even with high-throughput means to profile different materials, mapping the observations between studies in such a high-dimensional space can be difficult.

Systems biology, in conjunction with materials science, is well-suited for addressing this challenge. It integrates the combined effects of physical and biological processes involved in the interactions between cells, chemicals, materials and other biophysical and biochemical stimuli. Systems biology techniques encompass experimental and theoretical approaches to measure and/or predict the function of systems as an integrated unit (Box 1). Through assessment of patient samples, systems biology can help understand complex in vivo living systems and unravel the properties of and relationships between cells, tissues, organs, physiological systems and diseases.91,92. This information can then be used to design living material platforms, that can recapitulate the key physiological or pathophysiological processes and evaluate therapeutic interventions i93 (FIG. 3).

sec.title: Mechanistic modelling
sec.p: Mechanistic approaches, also referred to as physics, prior knowledge or first principles-based models, are commonly applied to the study of cancer and its tissue microenvironment. Many of these models explicitly consider the response of cancer tissue to extrinsic stimuli, including chemical, mechanical and other environmental cues, as a driver of ECM remodelling, cell-ECM adhesion, cell-cell adhesion and cancer-stroma communication (for example, fibroblasts, immune cells). Mechanistic models fall into two broad categories: deterministic models and stochastic models. Deterministic models typically include ordinary or partial differential equations that describe the dynamics of molecular concentrations, cell populations and/or spatiotemporal interactions. Deterministic models have been developed for the TME, in which cancer cells interact with stromal and immune cells or are impacted by other chemical and physical aspects of the microenvironment. Such deterministic models have been used to study signalling between cancer cells and diverse cells types or the ECM in the TME94–100, penetration of therapeutics and/or nutrients through the TME101–103, and migration of tumour cells through the TME104–108. Living materials that mimic the TME can incorporate the tunable mechanical properties of the ECM109, such as stiffness110, viscoelastic responses111,112 and cell-matrix adhesions113,114, which can be captured by mechanistic models of forces and biomechanics114–123.

In contrast to deterministic models, stochastic models include probabilistic effects to incorporate biological variability. Although stochastic versions of differential equations can be formulated, agent-based models (ABMs) are the more prevalent type of stochastic models in cancer systems biology. Complex computational platforms are available for ABMs to capture multicellular processes on the scale of tumour or organoid models. ABMs use rule-based components that determine the behaviors of discrete agents (often cells of one or more types) in response to their environment. Although ABM rules are not strictly stochastic, many formulations incorporate randomness into the rules to account for interactions of cellular agents with themselves, the microenvironment and other agents or factors; for example, stochasticity may arise in the movement of cellular agents, the likelihood of cell division, or the probability of receptor-ligand engagement. Thus, ABMs can be applied for the mechanistic modelling of cancer, considering multicellular effects and combinations of effects, such as pathway variations, spatial effects, motions, forces, chemical interactions and other phenotypic switches. In addition, ABMs can be combined with deterministic equations in an approach referred to as ‘hybrid modelling’, enabling the inclusion of prior knowledge of signaling pathways and other regulatory processes in the agent decision making124. ABMs have been used to study tumour interactions with biomaterials or with stromal and/or immune cellular communities121–123,125–140, and in the context of tumour growth, metastasis and treatment outcome 126,139,141,142. Emergent behaviors, such as coordination between agents, are not directly preprogrammed in ABMs; however, these models can recapitulate complex in vivo living systems and provide new insights, such as the role of angiogenesis in tumour development and chemotherapeutic responses143. For example, the ARCADE (Agent-based Representation of Cells And Dynamic Environments) platform explores differences in heterogeneity arising from colony culture versus tissue growth and the role of crowd tolerance and heterogeneity in the growth dynamics of competing clonal populations 144.

Living materials can be designed as in vitro models of cancer cell behavior to inform and parameterize ABMs, which, in turn, provide insight into putative biophysical mechanisms occurring in vivo. For example, an iterative systems biology process (FIG. 3) has been applied to investigate how microenvironmental stiffness modulates the growth properties of bone marrow stromal cells (BMSC) to support multiple myeloma initiating cells (MICs) and protect the MICs from drug sensitivity. Following the characterization of BMSC-myeloma interactions in an in vitro co-culture system, identifying intercellular crosstalk through CXCR4 145, the impact of collagen stiffness and cytocompression on a mechanotransduction feedback loop was revealed between the two cell types 146. These observations were then incorporated into rule-sets for biomechanical interactions between BMSCs and MICs that impact MIC transitions into mature and terminal multiple myeloma cells and subsequent niche remodeling in a simulated bone marrow microenvironmental niche 147. The spatial distribution of microenvironmental stiffness and proliferating MICs from the model were then quantitatively compared to experimental images obtained by 3D levitated co-culture. This integrated modelling-experimental approach identified a drug synergism that disrupts BMSC-MIC interactions and niche stiffness.

Experiments and agent-based modelling can also be combined to investigate cell migration. For example, live-cell microscopy was applied to study contact inhibition of locomotion of epithelial cells derived from a rat kidney (NRK-52E cell line), revealing that cells repolarize to change the direction of motion after collision 148. This type of cell behavior can influence cancer progression 149. Importantly, contact inhibition of locomotion is probabilistic and promoted by different types of cell-cell collisions, which can be modelled using an ABM to systematically investigate factors that influence this behavior. The ABM model predicted that the frequency of repolarization and collective migration of cells increase with the length of the train of cells involved in the collision, which was also experimentally validated. Building on these findings, a 3D micropatterned tumour model was designed to investigate how the ECM surrounding breast cancer cells influences repolarization and collective cell migration 150. Such studies can inform the design of responsive biomaterials that control cell behavior.

sec.title: Data-driven modelling
sec.p: Data-driven computational methods rely on the recognition of patterns within data, leveraging data science to interpret biology without necessarily presupposing some structure to the relationships between inputs and observations. Identifying such patterns can help to reduce, explore and visualize the effect of many different factors within living materials151. Multi-modal measurements (for example, measurements across dimensionality, stiffness and ECM content) can further benefit from generalizations of more traditional dimension-reduction techniques. For example, tensor-based methods, also referred to as context-dependent dimensionality reduction, can be effective at reducing data to specific patterns and separating the effect of each mode152, and are especially useful in capturing patterns in longitudinal (time-dependent) data. This benefit has been demonstrated in models of antibody responses and microbiome communities, in which the effects of antigen binding and immune receptor interaction, or time and subject, must be separated for effective interpretation153,154. Similarly, these types of methods should enable more effective exploration and manipulation of living materials.

Data-driven systems approaches have provided insights into the TME and biomaterials, for example, with regards to reciprocal signalling between tumour cells and stroma94; these types of interactions could be monitored or programmed into living materials. Similarly, the design of a bone tissue ECM-mimicking hydrogel was facilitated by data-driven modelling that integrated proteomics data to reveal a protein signature that was then included in the synthesis of living materials45. Moreover, a data-driven approach has been applied to screen drug resistance to microenvironmental cues151.

Several consortia are unifying quantitative experimental systems biology studies to generate large-scale data that is amenable to modelling, particularly for data-driven approaches, including ligand-mediated responses155, ECM protein constituents156 and senescence157, which has relevance to tumour cell dormancy.

sec.title: Future directions
sec.p: Prediction, optimization and control are potential roles that systems biology can play in informing living materials design and function. For example, dynamic input-output relationships and their associated network of effects and interactions are used in quantitative systems pharmacology and physiologically-based pharmacokinetics-pharmacodynamics modelling158. These approaches provide predictions of how to adjust and optimize pharmaceutical doses (inputs to the biological system) and their timing to achieve desired behaviors. Such systems biology approaches could also be used to control in vitro systems with complex interacting components and to leverage limited in vivo measurements to ensure the in vitro model is representative of the in vivo scenario. For example, systems biology models could be developed for organ-on-a chip and organoid platforms159 to further support and validate their use in predicting in vivo outcomes160 in a way similar to in vitro-to-in vivo correlation161. Similarly, the question of simplicity versus complexity of in vitro models, that is, what is the minimal complex model to faithfully represent the physiology or pathology for a particular tissue or a disease state, could be assessed using systems biology approaches.

Systems biology models could be used to predict therapeutic stimuli that elicit living material responses; for example, nanoparticles that mediate remodelling of the TME and stimulate immune interactions in tumours162. In addition, models have been applied to assess optimal drug penetration into the TME103 and the pharmacokinetics of a drug that elicits an anti-angiogenic response in tumours163. Moreover, the combination of mechanistic modelling (deterministic differential equations) and a data-driven approach have allowed the optimization of combined virotherapy and immunotherapy release from hydrogel materials to activate an anti-tumour immune response164. In addition, ABMs have been applied to design chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapeutics with desired interactions in culture and tissue-like environments165.

Purely data-driven modelling approaches might also be able to infer mechanistic interactions166. For example, a mechanistic model was generated from a large panel of perturbations and cellular responses (i.e., protein level and phenotypic changes) using a melanoma cell line, which was then used to infer regulatory interactions from unmeasured perturbation conditions167. Similarly, the intertwined effects of material perturbations could be inferred by including the function of a living material in the model building process. Thereby, the model could be used not only to identify new interactions, but also to update the materials based on new experimental observations 168. Furthermore, readouts from living materials sensors that are embedded in vivo could be coupled to systems biology models to predict dynamic responses to the measurements (FIG. 3). By identifying which environmental factors influence each other, these methods could predict the properties of living materials that should be manipulated to achieve desired goals. Therefore, data on the characterization and responses of living materials in different conditions need to be implemented in in silico models to leverage the power of systems biology for the rationale design of living materials.

sec.title: Cancer-specific applications of living materials
sec.p: Synthetic living materials can be used to engineer tumours and investigate cancer biology and therapies, and to predict personalized responses to therapies. Various preclinical cancer models, for example, microphysiological systems (MPS), have been developed to emulate the biochemical and biomechanical properties of a tumour ex vivo169–171 and to accurately and rapidly identify tumour vulnerabilities172; however, the question remains of how much complexity is needed to predict the relevant biological phenomena of investigation. Living materials and their integration with various types of sensors 173 may be a promising path toward elucidating the crucial tumour elements that need to be recapitulated ex vivo.

sec.title: Living materials and tumour heterogeneity
sec.p: The generation of heterotypic living materials comprising multiple cell types and mimicking the physical and chemical environment of tumour tissue has enabled investigations of tumour biology and therapeutic efficacy in the context of complex environments. Platforms can be engineered to assess the effects of different cell types 174–176, altered oxygen availability177, gradients of signalling factors23,178 and altered matrix composition or stiffness179–182 on tumour phenotypes and response to therapy. However, most of these models are static and can thus not account for changes to the environment surrounding neoplastic cells, which also affect response to drug treatments and cancer progression169–171,183. Therefore, living materials with dynamic, responsive properties are imperative for applications in cancer, which is a complex and adaptive disease. Living biomaterials, including hydrogels with reversible mechanical and thermal properties, can support mechanistic investigations into cancer initiation and progression 184–186. For example, hydrogel materials that allow the tuning of matrix mechanics revealed the impact of spatiotemporal microenvironmental changes on cellular plasticity, for example, those that influence cancer stem cell phenotype during melanoma and breast cancer progression 187. Gelatin-hyaluronic acid (HA) hybrid hydrogels with an enzyme-triggering matrix stiffening feature can trigger pancreatic cancer proliferation and EMT 188. 170,183182Thus, the complexity and dynamics should be included in preclinical model platforms to evaluate cancer phenotypes and test therapeutic responses in microenvironments with distinct and dynamically changing physical 186,187,189,190 or chemical properties.

sec.title: Living Materials and the TME
sec.p: Living materials can be applied to study the dynamic interplay between the TME and tumour cells. In particular, mechanotransduction, that is, the mechanism by which cells convert mechanical stimuli into biochemical signals, is a key factor in tumour progression 191. The dynamic nature of mechanical cues and their impact on cellular behavior can be modelled in living materials to investigate how cells adapt to changes in mechanical stimuli over time 192. Such living materials can be designed to respond and adapt to alterations in mechanical properties 193. For example, to account for the rapidly changing nature of CAFs and other stromal cells in tumours, nascent ECM protein secretion and remodeling can be tracked using proteolytically degradable covalently crosslinked HA hydrogels to evaluate tumour cell behaviors related to mechanosensing.

However, to develop such models, the minimal components (cellular and extracellular) that are required for living materials and patient-derived cells to self-organize and remodel their surroundings need to be defined. Non-destructive evaluation methods are essential for examining the resulting phenotypes. For example, cellular responses to perturbations induced by living material platforms can be assessed by examining extracellular vesicles (EVs) released from cells. Cells respond to mechanical stimuli from the ECM by altering their state 194 and by communicating with the surrounding environment through the release of EVs, such as exosomes 195. These exosomes can be quantified and characterized to investigate changes in intercellular communication caused by ECM-mediated changes. For example, a tunable, 3D biomimetic model of pancreatic adenocarcinoma showed that CAFs activated by a stiff, collagen-rich ECM increase the release of chemoresistance-promoting exosomes 196. Similarly, in tunable ECM scaffolds, breast cancer cells increase exosome secretion in response to an increase in matrix stiffness 197. Therefore, EV characterization may serve as a readout of cellular changes in response to the biophysical stimuli present in the TME, which can be emulated using living materials.

Furthermore, biosensors and feedback loops can be incorporated in living materials to enable real-time monitoring and control of environmental changes to study their effects on cellular behavior and therapeutic responses. For example, enzymes, chemical reductants and light-sensitive components can be implemented in a stimuli-responsive hydrogel system that contains orthogonal stimuli-labile linkages between small molecules and non-degradable materials to create programmable responses through YES, OR and AND logic gates. This platform allows the environmentally triggered release of therapeutics in response to cellular behavior 198. This type of responsive living material could also be employed to study how the TME controls cell plasticity, which is crucial for cancer progression, metastasis and therapy resistance.

By incorporating specific stimuli-responsive components that mimic the dynamic and complex nature of the TME, the physical and chemical properties of living materials can be manipulated in a spatiotemporal manner to examine how changes in the TME, such as alterations in ECM stiffness or the presence of specific signalling molecules, influence cellular plasticity, including the transition between epithelial and mesenchymal states, the emergence of cancer stem cell phenotypes, or the adaptation of cancer cells to cell-extrinsic factors. Furthermore, the integration of biosensors that detect specific signalling molecules or cellular activities could provide insight into how cellular communication is altered as the TME changes, increasing our understanding of tumour progression and resistance mechanisms.

sec.title: Living materials and tumour evolution
sec.p: Living materials can be used to explore the evolvability of tumours as disease progresses. A major challenge in studying tumour evolution is the scarcity of longitudinal patient data and samples. Living materials could provide valuable tools in the creation of a detailed and dynamic spatiotemporal atlas of a tumour to map the evolving interactome in a patient-specific manner. For example, synthesized materials (such as, nanoparticles 199, DNA sensors200, pH-sensitive reporters201–203) or biomaterials (such as bacterial or engineered cells204) could record and/or report localized mechanical and biochemical microenvironmental features within normal tissues to investigate structure-function relationships under non-pathological conditions. These platforms could then be used to dissect the changes that occur in the tissue and material as the tissue structure breaks down in response to tumourigenesis and disease progression. Such information would provide insight into the structural changes of the TME following tumour resection to identify targets to prevent growth of remaining tumour cells and subsequent disease recurrence.

Living materials could also be used to understand cell-cell interaction dynamics within tumours during different stages of disease progression. For example, engineered cells containing a molecular transfer system (the G-baToN system) allow recording of cancer cell-T cell interactions both in vitro and in vivo205. This nanobody-directed fluorescent labeling system allows monitoring of cell-cell interactions and transfer of cargo between cells based on physical contact, where surface GFP on tumor cells can be transferred to T cells expressing an anti-GFP nanobody when they touch. Living materials could also be used to probe the emergence of therapy resistance. For example, tumour evolution and dissemination to metastatic sites can be monitored using cancer cells programmed with an internal doxycycline inducible lineage recorder (macsGESTALT)206 that allows recording of cell lineage and single cell transcriptomics in vivo, demonstrating how living materials can be engineered to enable dynamic monitoring of single cell behavior as disease progression occurs. Multiple living materials could also be combined to explore the progression of clonal evolution and metastatic dissemination in response to endogenous stressors (such as hypoxia, immune cell interactions) versus exogenous stressors, such as the presence of a therapeutic.

sec.title: Synthetic biology-based design
sec.p: Synthetic biology can be applied in the design of living materials for several cancer-related applications including improved drug delivery, dosing, and TME modulation 207 (FIG. 4). In particular, control systems as well as ecological and population modelling may inform the dynamic regulation of drug dosing to keep solid tumours in check208,209; for example, instead of attempting to ‘cure’ a patient, a high-quality of life and extension of survival could be achieved in the treatment of late-stage metastatic prostate cancer by repeated low, subtoxic doses of chemotherapies210. Living materials could act as synthetic depots or reservoirs for the repeated autonomous dosing of therapeutic compounds. For example, genetic circuits designed for bacterial quorum sensing can be exploited to design non-motile Salmonella typhimurium that lyse synchronously and release cytotoxic chemotherapies at a threshold population density. Following oral delivery of circuit-engineered bacteria combined with chemotherapy, a significant reduction in tumour activity was observed within a syngeneic liver metastases mouse model211. Similarly, tumours colonized with engineered bacteria that encode the release of a nanobody CD47 antagonist show increased levels of tumor infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) and rapid regression of volume212; here, the engineered circuit mimics the overexpression of an anti-phagocytic receptor common to cancer cells that triggers anti-tumour immunity.

Synthetic biology can also be applied to improve immunotherapy efficacy through modulation of the metabolic TME213. Bacteria can be engineered to increase intratumoural L-arginine levels by continuously converting ammonia to L-arginine in MC38 colon cancer tumours, resulting in improved responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors by increasing the number of infiltrating T cells 214. Moreover, ‘smart’ chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapies can be designed using living materials. To improve the efficacy of CAR-T cell therapies in the treatment of solid tumours, the TME can be modulated, for example, by triggering proteolytic activity in conjunction with cancer antigen recognition; for example, CAR-T cells can be designed to express heparinase (HPSE) to degrade the ECM and promote tumour T cell infiltration and activity within neuroblastoma and melanoma xenograft models215. Alternatively, bio-orthogonal click chemistry can be applied to add ECM-degrading hyaluronidase and an anti-programmed death-ligand (PDL) 1 antibody to the surface of CAR-T cells to increase solid tumour T-cell infiltration and therapeutic efficacy216. ‘Masked’ CAR-T cells have also been designed that require TME proteases that cleave a probody peptide linker to reveal an active CAR at the desired tumour site217. The context-specific triggering of CAR-T cells within tumour environments has been the focus of ‘prime-and-kill’ synthetic Notch (synNotch) strategies; here, exploiting combinatorial antigen targets with Boolean AND or NOT logic gates can improve the tumour specificity of CAR-T cells218. Signal integration can be performed from tumour microenvironmental features, such as hypoxia or low pH; for example, a tumour hypoxia sensor can be designed through cell surface presentation of a multichain CAR with hypoxia inducible factor (HIF) 1a subdomains to conditionally discriminate and kill cancer cells219, albeit with limited effectiveness. 220

Synthetic biological engineering can also be applied to non-immune cells to model and therapeutically alter the TME. For example, immunomodulation can be achieved by introducing logic operator circuits into tumour cells. RNA-based circuits can be designed to induce the secretion of chemokine (C-C motif) ligand 21 (CCL21), interleukin-12 (IL-12) and an anti-PD1 antibody in tumour cells, and simultaneous presentation of surface T cell engager proteins (anti-CD3 single-chain variable fragment [scFv])) leads to the local activation of T cells in vitro and in vivo 221. The circuit outputs can be designed to induce a variety of immunomodulatory combinations, making this approach useful for testing across multiple cancer typess. Instead of introducing immune cell signaling components to elicit a response to a target antigen, a cell-contact sensing device222 can be designed in nonimmune cells with tumour tropism (e.g., mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and neural stem cells (NSCs). This synthetic construct employs an ON/OFF switch for the interleukin signaling cascade whereby cell contact is detected by antigen binding to scFv linked to a truncated interleukin receptor. The intracellular domain of the interleukin receptor elicits Janus kinase/signal transducers and activators of transcription (JAK/STAT6) signalling and induction of a pro-drug in vitro. A cell-penetrating enzyme then activates the drug in a tumour site-localized manner. Whether this system may result in off-target killing of sensor cells, secreting cells or tumour cells remains unclear; however, engineering nonimmune cell populations may allow the design of therapeutic sensing-and-release reservoirs within a variety of tissues.

sec.title: Outlook
sec.p: Transferring tools and approaches between systems biology, materials science, chemistry, engineering and synthetic biology will facilitate innovations in synthetic living materials. Materials engineering should be guided by systems biology to define the design space for distinct cancer applications. In addition, artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools to mine, analyze, and model material structure-function data, when combined with high-throughput synthesis technologies may allow the creation of iterations of materials with distinct properties at an accelerated and unprecedented scale . However, such materials will need to be validated by systems-level analytical tools that can assess high-content data across spatial and temporal scales.

Living material fabrication, including the choice of biomaterials, cellular components and environmental cues, needs to be standardized to ensure consistency. Strict quality control measures should be established for cellular components, such as cell authentication, mycoplasma testing and assessment of functional properties 223. Inter-laboratory validation studies can further help improve the reproducibility and reliability of living materials in cancer research 224. Sharing standardized protocols, materials and data between research groups can identify and address sources of variability, ultimately contributing to the development of robust, reproducible and transferrable living materials. Moreover, scalability plays a crucial role in enabling high-throughput drug screening and tailoring personalized medicine approaches. By leveraging techniques, such as microfluidics, 3D bioprinting and modular scaffold design, scalable living material systems can be developed that preserve the intricate biological features necessary for accurate cancer research.

Data analysis methods will be needed for assessing living materials given their temporal dynamics, which may or may not overlay with the temporal dynamics of embedded cells and tissues. Iterative design, evaluation and validation will be required to identify specific regulatory nodes and inform the programming of synthetic materials with therapeutic or diagnostic functions. High-throughput screening, automation and data-driven algorithms can accelerate system iterations and enable the identification of system perturbations in tumour model systems that produce specific functional changes in cell behavior. Similar approaches can be used for the design and synthesis of new modular materials, in particular, to engineer interchangeable material building blocks with specific functionalities, which can then be assembled as needed to enable specific living materials.

In parallel, advances in synthetic biology will allow the creation of cells and tissues that are microenvironmentally responsive and that can be paired with living materials; for example, synthetic biology components can be engineered in mammalian systems to integrate multiple external stimuli in a unique manner to impart novel functions, or to engineer specific response kinetics to a particular stimuli. Such synthetic circuits and parts could be designed at large scale that are transferable between different cell types. Moreover, synthetic circuits could be integrated into the genome of stem or progenitor cells which can then be differentiated into the required cell types, assuming that the synthetic circuits are maintained as cells transition between different differentiation states.

In addition to applications in cancer, living materials could be applied to study or modulate tissue repair, and to restore homeostasis in a variety of disease and injury contexts, for example, in wound healing, fibrosis, tissue integration of cell therapies and endogenous repair.

Applications and clinical translation of living materials will require targeted funding and community building initiatives to increase communication and tool translatability between the cell biology, material science, chemistry, engineering, systems biology and synthetic biology communities. These diverse communities must be trained to understand each other’s languages and communicate effectively. For example, training workshops in standardized computational platforms and data processing approaches to understand complex datasets and inform the design of living materials could be useful. Finally, as a community, we must commit to develop new technologies in an inclusive manner, ensuring that the designs are based on an understanding of how health and diseases manifest and impact humans from all racial and ethnic backgrounds, skin colors, sex and genders, and how socioeconomical and environmental forces shape health and diseases across communities. Genetic mutations that contribute to cancer have been correlated with ancestry225,226, and patient prognosis has been linked with racial disparities227,228. Racism is a public health crisis, and racial discrimination has been linked to somatic diseases229 and disparities in screening230,231. We must do better at integrating those aspects in our solutions and models. We need to include and fund232 researchers from diverse backgrounds and experiences to understand and solve grand challenges, and ultimately provide equitable and accessible solutions for all.

caption.title: Applications of living materials in cancer.
caption.p: Living materials could be applied to catalogue the tumour ecosystem in space and time to support the building of tumour atlases. Living materials further enable the creation of complex tumour culture models to understand the properties and rules of tumour ecosystems. Combining atlas data with data from complex culture models will enable the development of systems biology models to understand tumour dynamics and vulnerabilities. Ultimately, understanding the tumour ecosystem will inform the development of next-generation living therapies and tools for patient prognosis and therapy selection.

caption.title: Synthetic design of living materials.
caption.p: a) Tumour evolution, from ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) to metastasis, alongside remodeling of the tumour microenvironment by cancer associated fibroblasts (CAFs), their secreted cathepsins and matrix metalloproteases (MMPs), etc. Deposition and degradation of ECM proteins in the tumor microenvironment can both shield and attract tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) and other immune cell infiltration. b) Living materials made from synthetic starting materials can be used as cell culture environments and can be modified in response to triggers (for example, light, force, temperature and pH). These biomaterial changes can trigger phenotypic alterations in embedded cells, mirroring changes seen in the native tumor microenvironment. Activated cells within responsive biomaterials, such as CAFs, can degrade their surroundings via MMP/cathepsin secretion or pH changes. Living materials can be designed in such a way that the degraded material may then release bioactive, previously caged molecules, which can lead to a change of cell phenotypes to quiescent states or result in a new phenotype. Thus, the living systems evolves over time through dynamic, reciprocal interactions between biomaterials and cells. c) Living materials can dynamically crosslinked or stiffened through light (resulting in patterning of materials, if desired); through application of force, which can result in new crosslinks; pH and temperature, which can each trigger gelation through solvent-polymer interactions; and degradation or remodelling through proteolysis and presence of peptide/protein binding sites, respectively.

caption.title: Systems and synthetic biology in the design and analysis of living materials.
caption.p: Systems biology approaches of analysis and computational modelling can be used in the design and study of living materials. Analysis of patient tumours to determine the tumour composition and spatial organization can inform the design of living materials. Materials (for example, cell lines, organoids, immune cells and matrix components) derived from patient tumours can be incorporated into living materials to assess patient heterogeneity in phenotype and response. Living materials can also be manipulated to investigate how alterations in composition or perturbations of chemical or physical properties affect dynamic responses. Systems biology approaches of computational modelling can be performed to study tumours in vivo or in vitro. Iterating between experimentation with living materials, systems level analyses of the materials, and computational modelling of responses allows successive rounds of hypothesis generation and validation to gain insight into the dynamic phenotypes and responses of complex tumour ecosystems.

caption.title: Synthetic biology approaches to introduce smart cells into the tumour milieu.
caption.p: top) Colonization of tumours with quorum-sensing bacteria can trigger the release of lytic factors to keep tumours in check. Top middle) Engineered chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cells can be designed to release extracellular matrix (ECM)-degrading heparinase; bottom middle) in conjunction with cancer antigen recognition, this treatment may increase lymphocyte infiltration in the tumour microenviroment (TME). bottom) AND circuits built into either tumor cells or local stromal/immune cells that, upon external triggering (e.g. light) can release chemotherapy, targeted drugs, prodrugs, or a multitude of other small molecules or proteins that alter the phenotypic state of cells within.

boxed-text.label: BOX 1.
boxed-text.p: Systems biology is a conceptual approach to biomedical research that studies living systems as integrated units. This approach aims to identify how individual components, for example, genes, proteins or cells, work within the system to regulate behaviors on larger scales (cell, tissue and organism). The need for systems biology approaches arises from the observation that living systems rely on the intricate coordination of many molecular parts.

Systems biology is accomplished through the combined use of experiments and theoretical models. Experiments perturb individual parts of the system and measure responses to provide a more complete view of how distinct components interact. Such data can include omics-type measurements or a systematic collection of more focused measurements. Theoretical models typically leverage engineering, mathematics, physics and computer science approaches to develop a conceptual understanding of the system. These models can be categorized into mechanistic models, which apply existing knowledge of how a system works to model each component, and data-driven models, which use statistical patterns in experimental data to predict interactions.

The design and analysis of living materials for cancer research may benefit from systems biology investigations. Living materials are typically made from complex materials with many distinct molecular entities that can interact to provide new materials properties. The essential value of living materials comes through their integration and ability to sense and respond to their environment. Concepts from engineering and physics will provide a rich theoretical foundation on which to design and understand such responsive systems.

list-item.p: Living materials can be made of and by living cells or be completely synthetic with programmable elements catered to cells within.
Living materials are particularly useful for applications in cancer biology, because tumor microenvironments are highly dynamic and cell responsive.
Living materials can be designed by synthetic and systems biology to better model tumour heterogeneity and tumour evolution in response to therapy.

Future design and innovation on Living Materials requires inclusive design strategies and an understanding of how cancer impacts humans from all racial and ethnic backgrounds, skin colors, sex, and genders.
